power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Background: Eyes with open-angle glaucoma uncontrolled after a trabecular outflow procedure have limited options before progressing to bleb-forming surgery.
The uveoscleral pathway is distinct, relatively pressure-independent, and conjunctiva-sparing.
We report 12-month outcomes of standalone allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis in eyes with IOP that remained uncontrolled after prior trabecular outflow intervention.
Methods: Analysis of a multicentre registry (CREST; NCT05506423).
Eligible eyes had at least one prior trabecular outflow procedure, no prior bleb-forming surgery, and underwent uveoscleral outflow bio-intervention with at least 12 months of follow-up.
IOP reported as mean with 95% CI, medication as mean ± SD.
Results: Forty-seven eyes were eligible; 91.5% completed 12 months.
Consistent with moderateto-advanced glaucoma, baseline IOP was 22.5 mmHg (20.1, 24.9) on 3.0 (1.3) IOP-lowering medications, with visual field mean deviation -11.7 dB (8.1).
95.7% were pseudophakic.
In the per-protocol efficacy analysis, IOP fell 6.1 mmHg (3.7, 8.6), a 25.0% reduction (15.5%, 34.5%; p < 0.001), with no increase in medication.
text.formatted: In the per-protocol efficacy analysis, IOP fell 6.1 mmHg (3.7, 8.6), a 25.0% reduction (15.5%, 34.5%; p < 0.001), with no increase in medication.

text.text: At 12 months, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of freedom from incisional reoperation was 78.2% (61.8%, 88.2%).
There were no vision-threatening, clinically significant adverse events associated with the procedure such as persistent hypotony, maculopathy or other complications.

In eyes with inadequately controlled IOP following prior trabecular intervention, standalone allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis was associated with clinically meaningful IOP reduction without an increase in medication burden or permanent vision loss.
Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) remains the only intervention proven to slow glaucomatous progression 1 .
text.formatted: Lowering intraocular pressure (IOP) remains the only intervention proven to slow glaucomatous progression <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: The conventional (trabecular) outflow pathway, comprising the trabecular meshwork, Schlemm canal, collector channels and the episcleral venous system, carries the majority of aqueous and hosts the principal sites of pathological resistance in open-angle glaucoma (OAG) 2, 3 .
text.formatted: The conventional (trabecular) outflow pathway, comprising the trabecular meshwork, Schlemm canal, collector channels and the episcleral venous system, carries the majority of aqueous and hosts the principal sites of pathological resistance in open-angle glaucoma (OAG) <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: The unconventional (uveoscleral) pathway drains across the ciliary muscle face into the supraciliary and suprachoroidal spaces and is comparatively pressure-independent, functioning as a relief route whose capacity rises as trabecular resistance increases 3.
text.formatted: The unconventional (uveoscleral) pathway drains across the ciliary muscle face into the supraciliary and suprachoroidal spaces and is comparatively pressure-independent, functioning as a relief route whose capacity rises as trabecular resistance increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref>.

text.text: Pharmacologically, this pathway is the target of the most effective class of ocular hypotensive medication: prostaglandin analogues lower IOP principally by enhancing uveoscleral outflow 4 and produce the largest IOP reduction of any first-line medication 5, 6 .
text.formatted: Pharmacologically, this pathway is the target of the most effective class of ocular hypotensive medication: prostaglandin analogues lower IOP principally by enhancing uveoscleral outflow <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> and produce the largest IOP reduction of any first-line medication <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: This distinction has a direct therapeutic consequence.

Trabecular-based minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) can only reduce IOP down to the pressure set by distal resistance and episcleral venous pressure, which in practice imposes a post-trabecular IOP floor in the midteens 7, 8 .
text.formatted: Trabecular-based minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) can only reduce IOP down to the pressure set by distal resistance and episcleral venous pressure, which in practice imposes a post-trabecular IOP floor in the midteens <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: A level-I American Academy of Ophthalmology assessment of randomised data found that adding a trabecular procedure to cataract surgery yields only 1.6 to 2.3 mmHg (3.8% to 8.9%) of additional IOP reduction beyond the 5.4 to 7.6 mmHg (21% to 28%) provided by phacoemulsification itself 9 .
text.formatted: A level-I American Academy of Ophthalmology assessment of randomised data found that adding a trabecular procedure to cataract surgery yields only 1.6 to 2.3 mmHg (3.8% to 8.9%) of additional IOP reduction beyond the 5.4 to 7.6 mmHg (21% to 28%) provided by phacoemulsification itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Approximately three-quarters of the IOP reduction seen in combined cataract-MIGS is therefore attributable to the cataract extraction rather than the trabecular device.

When the lens contribution is removed, as in the pseudophakic, standalone setting, the ceiling of trabecular surgery becomes clinically apparent, and once that pathway has already been surgically manipulated and has failed, further trabecular intervention offers diminishing physiological returns.
For a pseudophakic eye with moderate-to-advanced glaucoma that remains uncontrolled after a prior trabecular procedure, this leaves a therapeutic gap.
The available options have historically been either another attempt at the same, already-compromised conventional pathway or an escalation to bleb-forming surgery.

Bleb-forming surgery is the most effective IOP-lowering approach but carries a lifelong risk of bleb-related complications, such as infection, hypotony and scarring-related failure, and consumes conjunctival tissue whose prior disturbance measurably lowers the success of any subsequent filtration procedure 1, 10, 11 .
text.formatted: Bleb-forming surgery is the most effective IOP-lowering approach but carries a lifelong risk of bleb-related complications, such as infection, hypotony and scarring-related failure, and consumes conjunctival tissue whose prior disturbance measurably lowers the success of any subsequent filtration procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> .

text.text: A conjunctivasparing option that addresses the untouched, complementary outflow pathway is therefore a useful intermediate step.
The uveoscleral (unconventional) outflow pathway is a physiologically distinct target.

It accounts for 35%-50% of total aqueous outflow in healthy adults and functions as a relatively pressure-independent route where aqueous humour traverses the ciliary muscle into the supraciliary and suprachoroidal spaces 12, 13 .
text.formatted: It accounts for 35%-50% of total aqueous outflow in healthy adults and functions as a relatively pressure-independent route where aqueous humour traverses the ciliary muscle into the supraciliary and suprachoroidal spaces <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: Prostaglandin analogues act predominantly along this pathway, lowering IOP through remodelling of ciliary muscle extracellular matrix 4, 14.
text.formatted: Prostaglandin analogues act predominantly along this pathway, lowering IOP through remodelling of ciliary muscle extracellular matrix <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref>.

text.text: Surgical attempts to harness the uveoscleral pathway date back to Heine's cyclodialysis procedure in 1905.
Despite its potent IOP-lowering potential, classic cyclodialysis fell out of favour due to unpredictable cleft closure and hypotony.

A recent systematic review and metaanalysis of over 4,000 glaucoma cases spanning 100 years of surgical experience found cyclodialysis to be effective in lowering IOP as a uveoscleral outflow-enhancing procedure, with modern ab-interno approaches showing improved efficacy, safety and procedural longevity compared with historical ab-externo techniques 15 .
text.formatted: A recent systematic review and metaanalysis of over 4,000 glaucoma cases spanning 100 years of surgical experience found cyclodialysis to be effective in lowering IOP as a uveoscleral outflow-enhancing procedure, with modern ab-interno approaches showing improved efficacy, safety and procedural longevity compared with historical ab-externo techniques <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Early attempts to stent the supraciliary space with synthetic materials (e.g., the CyPass Micro-Stent) confirmed the hydraulic efficacy of the pathway as a potent outflow channel, similar to the high therapeutic index seen with uveo-scleral IOP lowering agents such as prostaglandin analogues 16, 17.
text.formatted: Early attempts to stent the supraciliary space with synthetic materials (e.g., the CyPass Micro-Stent) confirmed the hydraulic efficacy of the pathway as a potent outflow channel, similar to the high therapeutic index seen with uveo-scleral IOP lowering agents such as prostaglandin analogues <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref>.

text.text: Allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis is a newer approach to uveoscleral outflow enhancement.

An allogeneic, acellular scleral bio-scaffold reinforces the cyclodialysis cleft, with the aim of promoting bio-integration instead of the fibrous encapsulation seen with synthetic supraciliary devices 18, 19 .
text.formatted: An allogeneic, acellular scleral bio-scaffold reinforces the cyclodialysis cleft, with the aim of promoting bio-integration instead of the fibrous encapsulation seen with synthetic supraciliary devices <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: This report presents 12-month outcomes of allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis performed as a standalone procedure in eyes with a history of prior trabecular intervention and inadequate IOP control on medical therapy, in a predominantly pseudophakic population.
>Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Methods</head>

text.text: The CREST Study (NCT05506423) is a multicentre, observational, real-world evidence registry, in which patients with OAG who underwent bio-interventional uveoscleral enhancement surgery with the AlloFlo Uveo™ System (Iantrek, Inc., White Plains, NY) are prospectively followed through 24 months postoperatively.
CREST is conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, with approval from relevant Institutional Review Boards for all participating investigators.
All participants provided written informed consent prior to enrolment.

This study analysed a subgroup of eyes from CREST Cohort 2 (allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis) meeting the following inclusion criteria: (1) history of at least one prior trabecular outflow intervention (defined as any of canaloplasty, trabecular stent implantation, goniotomy, trabeculotomy, or laser trabeculoplasty), (2) no prior conjunctival bleb-forming procedure (trabeculectomy, tube shunt, subconjunctival gel stent), (3) placement of two allogeneic scleral allografts during a single surgical session, and (4) the surgery had been performed at least 12 months before data cutoff for analysis.
As an uncontrolled subgroup analysis of a single-arm registry, this study is not designed to support comparative claims against alternative interventions.

Two minimally modified, homologous allograft spacers of processed, acellular scleral tissue (5 mm × 500 µm) were deployed into the supraciliary space to provide structural support and serve as a porous conduit for aqueous humour drainage into the uveoscleral pathway.
The allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis procedure was performed using an ab-interno approach under gonioscopic visualisation.
Elongated acellular scleral allograft tissue constructs were prepared and introduced into the anterior chamber (Figure 1) under gonio-visualisation (Figure 2).

text.text: The allografts were deployed at the endoscleral surface bilaterally and adjacent to the edges of the cyclodialysis.
Components did not protrude into the anterior chamber (AC), and AC-clear placement was confirmed under direct visualisation with the allografts deployed flush with the iris root.
Any residual viscoelastic was evacuated with irrigation or irrigation/aspiration.
Patients were prescribed a surgeon's choice of postoperative antibiotics and corticosteroids with taper.

text.text: Longitudinal changes in IOP and medication burden from baseline were tested using a paired ttest.
Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05.
text.formatted: Statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05.

text.text: IOP data are presented as means with 95% confidence intervals (95% CI); medications as means ± standard deviation (SD).
Responder rates are reported at IOP thresholds of ≤ 21, ≤ 18 and ≤ 15 mmHg and at ≥ 20% reduction from baseline.
Composite responder was defined as meeting the stated IOP threshold without an increase in glaucoma medications from baseline.
Time to reoperation was estimated by Kaplan-Meier analysis with complementary log-log confidence intervals.
Reoperation was defined as any incisional IOP-lowering procedure, and eyes without a reoperation were censored at their last scheduled study visit.

In a sensitivity analysis, any subsequent IOP-lowering procedure, including cyclophotocoagulation, laser trabeculoplasty and laser peripheral iridotomy, was counted as a failure; anterior chamber paracentesis was not.

For each protocol visit, mean IOP and mean medication burden were computed using all eyes with a measurement available in that visit's window, with per-visit N reported explicitly; no imputation was applied.

Consistent with reporting conventions for real-world registry analyses of glaucoma surgery outcomes 20 , eyes were censored from IOP and medication summary analyses at the time of any subsequent IOP-lowering procedure.

>Results

text.text: A total of 47 eyes (45 patients) met all inclusion criteria and were included for analysis (Table 1).

text.text: Thirty-two eyes had a Month 12 pressure recorded before undergoing any further pressurelowering procedure.
The remainder had already undergone a further procedure, so their later readings reflect that intervention rather than the index surgery.

The cohort was an advanced glaucoma population that had failed at least one prior canal/trabecular intervention: mean baseline medicated IOP was 22.5 mmHg (20.1, 24.9); eyes were on a mean (SD) 3.0 (1.3) topical IOP-lowering medications, with 61.7% on ≥ 3 medications; mean (SD) visual field mean deviation was -11.7 (8.1) dB.
Most eyes were pseudophakic (45 [95.7%]); one eye was phakic and one aphakic.
Five eyes (10.6%) were taking a systemic anticoagulant or antiplatelet agent.

At baseline, eyes had undergone the following prior trabecular interventions: laser trabeculoplasty (78.7%), canaloplasty (51.1%), trabecular stent implantation (19.1%), and goniotomy/trabeculotomy (14.9%).
Sixty-six per cent had undergone two or more prior trabecular or angle-based procedures and 27.7% three or more, counting each component of a combined procedure separately.

Eleven of 47 eyes (23.4%) underwent an incisional reoperation during the follow-up period.

Eight eyes (17.0%) proceeded to bleb-forming filtration, comprising a gel stent in five, trabeculectomy in two and an ExPRESS shunt in one, at a median of 190 days; three eyes (6.4%) received a glaucoma drainage device, at a median of 350 days.
The Kaplan-Meier estimate (95% CI) for freedom from reoperation at 12 months was 78.2% (61.8%, 88.2%) (Table 3, Figure 5).

text.text: Seventeen eyes remained at risk at 12 months.

Twenty-one eyes without a reoperation were censored before 12 months: 17 at a Month 12 visit held between days 277 and 365, 2 at their Month 1 or Month 6 visit, and 2 that had no scheduled follow-up visit.
Separately, four eyes (8.5%) underwent cyclophotocoagulation (five procedures) and two eyes (4.3%) underwent laser trabeculoplasty; no eye underwent laser peripheral iridotomy.
All seven procedures were performed for inadequate IOP control, in one case with poor adherence to medication noted, and four of them took place within the first 12 months.
One of the cyclophotocoagulation procedures preceded an incisional reoperation in the same eye.

When any subsequent IOP-lowering procedure was counted as a failure, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of freedom from further intervention at 12 months was 70.1% (52.8%, 82.1%), with 16 eyes at risk at 12 months (Table 3, Figure 6).

text.text: Incidental retinal complications over the 12-month follow-up period occurred in 2 eyes (4.3%): 1 retinal tear and 1 retinal detachment.
Both were assessed by the investigator as unrelated to the allograft or study procedure.
No eye in this cohort had a shallow chamber with iridocorneal apposition.
Postoperative gonioscopy was performed at least once in 30 eyes (63.8%).
Among those eyes, the allograft was recorded as optimally positioned in 27 (90.0%), and the cleft was open around the allograft in 3 (10.0%).
Partial synechiae around or over the allograft were recorded in 2 (6.7%) eyes.
None had total synechiae.

One eye had an adverse event of corneal endothelial touch by the allograft.

This eye had 274 previously undergone laser trabeculoplasty and three angle-based procedures and had 275 subsequently received cyclophotocoagulation and a gel stent; the finding was attributed by the 276 investigator to post-operative changes following those reinterventions.
Surgical trimming of the 277 allograft was performed, and the event was reported as resolved without sequelae.

In this CREST subgroup of 47 eyes uncontrolled after prior trabecular intervention, standalone allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis of the complementary uveoscleral pathway was associated with a 25.0% IOP reduction at 12 months (p < 0.001), achieved without an increase in medication burden, in an advanced population (61.7% on three or more medications, mean visual field mean deviation -11.7 dB, 95.7% pseudophakic).

text.text: Kaplan-Meier freedom from reoperation was 78.2%, or 70.1% when any further IOP-lowering procedure was counted as a failure, and there were no cases of clinically significant hypotony, which was the failure mode of unreinforced cyclodialysis.
The rationale for this approach is physiological.
Conventional and uveoscleral outflow are distinct systems with distinct rate-limiting resistances 2, 3 .
text.formatted: Conventional and uveoscleral outflow are distinct systems with distinct rate-limiting resistances <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> .

text.text: Trabecular procedures are constrained by resistance distal to the trabecular meshwork and by episcleral venous pressure, which together impose a practical IOP floor in the mid-teens and cannot be overcome by re-operating on the same route 7, 8 .
text.formatted: Trabecular procedures are constrained by resistance distal to the trabecular meshwork and by episcleral venous pressure, which together impose a practical IOP floor in the mid-teens and cannot be overcome by re-operating on the same route <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> .

text.text: In randomised studies, trabecular procedures have been shown to add only about 1.6 to 2.3 mmHg over cataract surgery, and roughly three-quarters of the reduction seen in combined procedures comes from the lens extraction 9 .
text.formatted: In randomised studies, trabecular procedures have been shown to add only about 1.6 to 2.3 mmHg over cataract surgery, and roughly three-quarters of the reduction seen in combined procedures comes from the lens extraction <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: In a pseudophakic eye that has already failed a trabecular intervention, both the lens contribution and much of the trabecular capacity have already been used.

Redirecting the surgical effort to the untouched, comparatively pressureindependent uveoscleral pathway is therefore a mechanistically distinct escalation rather than a repeat of a route that has already failed 4, 14 .

text.text: The preserved effect in the stricter non-laser subgroup (22.5% reduction, paired N=25) supports the interpretation that benefit derives from engaging a new pathway rather than from regression of prior laser effect.

Because it is ab-interno and leaves the conjunctiva undisturbed, allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis preserves the option of future bleb-forming surgery, whose success is degraded by prior conjunctival manipulation and scarring 1, 10 .

text.text: In a moderate-to-advanced cohort, many of whom will eventually need filtration, deferring conjunctival disturbance while still lowering IOP and avoiding added drops is a practical advantage in sequencing.

Cross-study comparisons with published trabecular MIGS series should be interpreted with substantial caution, because baseline characteristics such as prior surgery, baseline IOP, medication burden and lens status differ materially across cohorts and no head-to-head data exist.
IRIS Registry analyses have reported cumulative reoperation rates of 15%-24% at 2 years after standalone MIGS procedures 20 .
text.formatted: IRIS Registry analyses have reported cumulative reoperation rates of 15%-24% at 2 years after standalone MIGS procedures <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> .

text.text: In the present cohort, 11 of 47 eyes (23.4%) underwent reoperation during the observation window.

For context, a prospective single-arm study of standalone trabecular micro-bypass in eyes uncontrolled by prior surgical or medical therapy reported a mean diurnal IOP reduction of 5.9 mmHg at 12 months from a baseline of 23.4 mmHg on a mean of 3.1 medications, and 5.5 mmHg in the subgroup with prior failed surgery 21 .
text.formatted: For context, a prospective single-arm study of standalone trabecular micro-bypass in eyes uncontrolled by prior surgical or medical therapy reported a mean diurnal IOP reduction of 5.9 mmHg at 12 months from a baseline of 23.4 mmHg on a mean of 3.1 medications, and 5.5 mmHg in the subgroup with prior failed surgery <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: In the present cohort, the 32 eyes contributing a paired Month 12 measurement had a baseline IOP of 20.8 mmHg on a mean of 3.0 medications and a mean reduction of 6.1 mmHg.
Differences in IOP ascertainment, baseline pressure and study design preclude direct comparison.

These figures are offered as contextual background only, and direct comparative trials would be required to establish the relative position of allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis against trabecular MIGS.
Allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis produced meaningful standalone IOP reduction in eyes with prior trabecular intervention while leaving the conjunctiva intact for future filtering surgery.
In the surgical sequence it fits well between a second trabecular attempt and bleb-forming surgery.

First, this is a single-arm, non-randomised sub-study of a real-world evidence study of consecutive, prospectively followed subjects, in which each patient was treated with the postoperative standard of care as applied by their treating physician.
Selection bias and confounding are inherent to this observational design and cannot be fully controlled.

Second, the efficacy analysis is confined to the 32 eyes that contributed a Month 12 measurement before any subsequent IOP-lowering procedure, and the definition of disease control is not protocolised but assessed individually by the treating physicians' discretion.
Third, no medication washout was performed, so IOP and medication outcomes are interdependent.
The composite responder endpoint (IOP threshold met without added medication) is the most conservative reading and is reported for this reason.
Fourth, the "prior trabecular intervention" population was heterogeneous, dominated by laser trabeculoplasty.
The non-laser sensitivity analysis mitigates this but cannot eliminate it.
Fifth, the Kaplan-Meier estimates confidence intervals are relatively wide; the durability of overall success therefore could benefit from longer follow-up.
Finally, corneal endothelial data are sparse and available in only a fraction of patients, as specular microscopy is not standard of care in interventional glaucoma patients.

Key efficacy endpoints of interest included: mean medicated IOP over time, mean change in IOP from baseline to Month 12, mean change in medication burden, and responder rates.

Safety endpoints included the incidence of ocular adverse events, specifically clinically significant hypotony er) ) at baseline (N=47), 2.1 (1.6) at Month 1 (N=42), 2.7 (1.7) at Month 6 (N=37) and 2.8 (1.5) at Month 12 (N=32).

Among the 32 eyes evaluable at Month 12, mean medication burden was 2.97 (1.31) at baseline and 2.84 (1.46) at Month 12, a change of -0.12 (-0.50, +0.25), which was not statistically significant (p = 0.50).
The proportion of medication-free eyes was 4.3% (2 of 47) at baseline, 10.8% (4 of 37) at Month 6 and 3.1% (1 of 32) at Month 12.

The Month 1 proportion (16.7%) was artificially high due to the common clinical practice of temporarily withholding glaucoma medication in the early postoperative period.Corneal endothelial cell count was available at both baseline and Month 12 in 7 eyes (14.9%), reflecting that real-world specular microscopy is not required by the CREST protocol and not part of routine glaucoma care.

In eyes with evaluable ECC data, the mean was 2,002 cells/mm² at baseline and 2,060 cells/mm² at Month 12, a change of +59 cells/mm² (-72, +189; p = 0.31), or +3.9% (-2.4%, +10.1%); individual changes ranged from -7.2% to +9.5%.
